reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Asplenia syndrome is the visceral marker of right atrial isomerism (bilateral right-sidedness), characterised by congenital absence of the spleen and duplicated right-sided morphology.
Both lungs are trilobed with eparterial bronchi and both atrial appendages are of morphologically right type, features more reliable for classification than the absent spleen itself.
Cardiac disease is typically severe and cyanotic, with common atrioventricular canal, single ventricle physiology, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, and total anomalous pulmonary venous connection.
Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection, often obstructed, is a defining and life-threatening association demanding urgent recognition in the cyanotic neonate.
Absence of the spleen produces lifelong susceptibility to overwhelming encapsulated-organism sepsis, so prophylactic antibiotics and full vaccination are mandatory.
Howell-Jolly bodies and Heinz bodies on the blood film confirm the functional consequences of asplenia.
A symmetrical midline liver and intestinal malrotation are usual, the latter risking midgut volvulus.
Bilateral superior venae cavae and other systemic venous anomalies are common and complicate surgical and catheter approaches.
reference.pathophysiology: Asplenia syndrome results from a laterality defect in which the embryo fails to establish left-sided identity and instead duplicates right-sided morphology bilaterally. Failure of nodal cilia-generated leftward flow and of the downstream Nodal-Lefty-Pitx2 signalling cascade abolishes the normal asymmetry, so paired organs adopt right-sided features on both sides: the lungs become trilobed with eparterial bronchi and both atria carry morphologically right appendages. The spleen, a structure of left-sided embryonic origin, fails to develop, leaving the child functionally and anatomically asplenic and highly vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria. The same disturbance produces a midline symmetrical liver, anomalous systemic and pulmonary venous connections, and the severe conotruncal and atrioventricular septal malformations that dominate the clinical picture. Intestinal rotation, which depends on normal left-right cues, is likewise disordered.
additionalDifferentials: situs solitus with complex cyanotic congenital heart disease
isolated total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
additionalInvestigations: urgent segmental echocardiography including pulmonary venous drainage assessment
abdominal ultrasound confirming absent spleen and midline liver
peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly and Heinz bodies
chest imaging for bronchial morphology and pulmonary lobation
cardiac CT or MRI angiography for systemic and pulmonary venous mapping
twelve-lead ECG documenting atrial rhythm and axis
genetic evaluation for laterality and ciliopathy genes in selected cases
redFlags: profound neonatal cyanosis, especially with obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
fever or rapid clinical deterioration signalling overwhelming post-splenectomy-type sepsis
bilious vomiting or abdominal distension from midgut volvulus
duct-dependent circulation requiring urgent prostaglandin and intervention
shock or acidosis in an infant with known right isomerism
reference.prognosis: Asplenia syndrome carries the poorest prognosis among the heterotaxy variants because of severe cyanotic cardiac lesions, frequent obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, and the constant threat of fulminant sepsis. Survival has improved with early surgical palliation and rigorous infection prophylaxis, but morbidity and mortality remain high and many follow a single-ventricle pathway.
pitfalls: Failing to search for obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection in the cyanotic neonate.
Not recognising the absent spleen and omitting antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccination.
Classifying by spleen status alone rather than bronchial and atrial appendage morphology.
Overlooking intestinal malrotation until volvulus occurs.
Underestimating systemic venous anomalies during surgical or catheter planning.
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
American Heart Association scientific statement on heterotaxy
management: Staged surgical palliation of the complex cyanotic cardiac lesions, typically along a single-ventricle pathway, by paediatric cardiac surgery
Urgent surgical repair of obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection in the cyanotic neonate
Lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms and prompt empirical antibiotics for any febrile illness, given the functional asplenia
Comprehensive immunisation including pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines
Vigilance for intestinal malrotation with volvulus and other heterotaxy-associated visceral anomalies, with surgical correction where indicated
Multidisciplinary follow-up by paediatric cardiology with serial echocardiography, and family and genetic counselling for the underlying laterality defect
A clear escalation plan and family education for early recognition of overwhelming sepsis
